```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7.5,
                      fig.height = 4.2, fig.retina = 2, out.width = "100%",
                      fig.align = "center")
has_stan <- requireNamespace("cmdstanr", quietly = TRUE) &&
  !is.null(tryCatch(cmdstanr::cmdstan_path(), error = function(e) NULL))
cols <- c("#4F6D8F", "#C8553D", "#E0A458", "#5B8E7D")
```

In `phylogp` a model of trait evolution *is* its kernel: the covariance it
implies between species. This vignette shows how to look at kernels, build
new ones, and check that they are valid before fitting anything. Apart
from one optional fit, nothing here needs Stan.

```{r}
library(phylogp)
set.seed(12)
tr <- ape::rphylo(30, birth = 1, death = 0)      # a pure-birth tree
tr$edge.length <- tr$edge.length / max(ape::node.depth.edgelength(tr))
```

## The building blocks

The components correspond to familiar models: Brownian motion
[@felsenstein1985], Pagel's transformations [@pagel1999], early burst
[@blomberg2003; @harmon2010], Ornstein–Uhlenbeck [@hansen1997; @butler2004],
autocorrelated rates [@thorne2002; @eastman2011; @venditti2011] and
distance-based kernels as used for spatial structure [@freckleton2009;
@hartmann2023]. `k_white()` is the species-level variation of the
phylogenetic mixed model [@lynch1991; @housworth2004]. Kernels are combined
by sums and products, as is usual for Gaussian processes
[@rasmussen2006; @duvenaud2013].

| Component | Kernel (before scaling by `sigma^2`) | Form |
|---|---|---|
| `k_bm()` | shared path length $t_{ij}$ | branch-wise |
| `k_lambda()` | $\lambda t_{ij}$, tip variance kept | branch-wise |
| `k_kappa()` | branch lengths raised to $\kappa$ | branch-wise |
| `k_delta()` | $T^{1-\delta} t_{ij}^{\delta}$ | branch-wise |
| `k_eb()` | $(e^{r t_{ij}} - 1)/r$ | branch-wise |
| `k_ou()` | $e^{-\alpha d_{ij}}/2\alpha$ (random root) | branch-wise on ultrametric trees |
| `k_relaxed()` | rate evolves by BM along the tree | branch-wise, latent rates |
| `k_rate_time()` | rate a smooth function of time | branch-wise, latent rates |
| `k_white()` | independent tip variance; `df =` for Student-t | tip |
| `k_slope(x) * k` | slope on `x` evolving under `k`: $x_i x_j k(i, j)$ | latent (linear) or dense |
| `k_dist()` | $\phi(D_{ij}/\ell)$ on any distance | dense |
| `k_edge()` | **your own** edge variances | branch-wise |

Components are added with `+`, and a branch-wise component can be multiplied
by a covariate with `k_slope()` (see `vignette("slopes-prediction")`). A sum describes independent processes
acting together, for example phylogeny, space and residual variation:

```{r}
k_bm() + k_dist(phi = "exponential") + k_white()
```

*Branch-wise* components add variance along the edges of the tree. Any sum
of them keeps the linear-time pruning likelihood [@felsenstein1973; @ho2014];
adding a dense component
switches the model to dense linear algebra.

## A gallery of kernels

The same tree seen through six kernels. Each matrix shows the correlation
between species, with tips in tree order, so clades show up as blocks.

```{r gallery, fig.height = 5.6}
# a clade of about 8 species evolving 5 times faster, for k_relaxed()
clade <- 30 + which.min(abs(lengths(ape::prop.part(tr)) - 8))
below <- function(node) c(node, unlist(lapply(tr$edge[tr$edge[, 1] == node, 2], below)))
z <- numeric(30 + tr$Nnode)
z[below(clade)] <- log(5)
gallery <- list(
  "Brownian motion"         = list(k_bm(), NULL),
  "Pagel's lambda = 0.5"    = list(k_lambda(), list(lambda1 = list(lambda = 0.5))),
  "Early burst (r = -3)"    = list(k_eb(), list(eb1 = list(rate = -3))),
  "OU (alpha = 3)"          = list(k_ou(), list(ou1 = list(alpha = 3))),
  "Relaxed rates"           = list(k_relaxed(), list(relaxed1 = list(z = z))),
  "Squared exponential"     = list(k_dist(phi = "sqexp"), list(dist1 = list(ell = 0.5)))
)
op <- par(mfrow = c(2, 3), mar = c(0.5, 0.5, 2, 0.5))
for (nm in names(gallery))
  kernel_plot(gallery[[nm]][[1]], tr, pars = gallery[[nm]][[2]],
              main = nm, show_tree = FALSE)
par(op)
```

## Simulating from a kernel

`kernel_simulate()` draws traits from a kernel: a quick way to see what
data a model expects (a prior predictive check).

```{r simulate, fig.height = 4.4}
trait_plot <- function(tree, y, main, col) {
  H <- max(ape::node.depth.edgelength(tree))
  ape::plot.phylo(tree, show.tip.label = FALSE, x.lim = c(0, 1.75 * H),
                  edge.color = "grey45", main = main, cex.main = 1, font.main = 1)
  lp <- get("last_plot.phylo", envir = ape::.PlotPhyloEnv)
  tips <- seq_along(tree$tip.label)
  x0 <- 1.38 * H
  y <- y - mean(y)                      # deviations from the mean
  v <- y[tree$tip.label] / max(abs(y)) * 0.33 * H
  segments(x0, lp$yy[tips], x0 + v, lp$yy[tips], lwd = 3.5, lend = 1,
           col = ifelse(v > 0, col, adjustcolor(col, 0.45)))
  segments(x0, 0.5, x0, length(tips) + 0.5, col = "grey60")
}
set.seed(11)
op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 3), mar = c(0.5, 0.5, 2.5, 0.5))
trait_plot(tr, kernel_simulate(k_bm(), tr)[, 1], "Brownian motion", cols[1])
trait_plot(tr, kernel_simulate(k_eb(), tr, list(eb1 = list(rate = -5)))[, 1],
           "Early burst", cols[2])
trait_plot(tr, kernel_simulate(k_ou(), tr, list(ou1 = list(alpha = 6)))[, 1],
           "Ornstein-Uhlenbeck", cols[4])
par(op)
```

Under an early burst, differences arise deep in the tree and whole clades
differ; under strong OU selection, close relatives can differ as much as
distant ones.

## Writing your own kernel

Most new models of trait evolution are just a new rule for how much
variance each branch accumulates. `k_edge()` takes that rule as a Stan
expression of the edge length `len`, the heights of the start and end of the
edge `hs` and `he`, the indicator `is_tip`, the tree height `Tmax`, and your
own parameters. Here is Pagel's κ combined with a rate that changes
exponentially through time:

```{r custom}
k_trend <- k_edge("pow(len, kappa) .* exp(beta * he)",
                  pars = list(kappa = c(0, 1), beta = c(-5, 5)),
                  name = "trend")
k_trend
```

A kernel of this branch-wise form is a valid covariance on *every* tree, as
long as its edge variances are non-negative. `kernel_check()` verifies this
over a grid of parameter values:

```{r custom-check}
kernel_check(k_trend, tr)
```

A careless rule is caught:

```{r custom-bad}
kernel_check(k_edge("len + beta * he", pars = list(beta = c(-5, 5))), tr)
```

The custom kernel goes into the generated Stan program unchanged, so it
keeps the linear-time likelihood:

```{r custom-code}
code <- strsplit(kernel_stancode(k_trend + k_white()), "\n")[[1]]
cat(code[grep("= trend1_kappa;", code, fixed = TRUE)[1] + (-2:3)], sep = "\n")
```

and it can be fitted like any built-in kernel:

```{r custom-fit, eval = has_stan, message = FALSE}
big <- ape::rcoal(150)
big$edge.length <- big$edge.length / max(ape::node.depth.edgelength(big))
y <- kernel_simulate(k_trend, big,
                     pars = list(trend1 = list(kappa = 0.6, beta = -3)))[, 1]
fit <- phylo_gp(y ~ 1, data = data.frame(y = y, row.names = names(y)),
                tree = big, kernel = k_trend, method = "optimize")
fit
```

## Is my kernel valid?

A kernel must be positive semi-definite on the tips of the tree, or it is
not a covariance at all. It is tempting to plug patristic distances into
the squared-exponential kernel that most Gaussian-process software uses by
default. Whether that works depends on the tree:

* On an **ultrametric** tree any non-increasing function of patristic
  distance is valid: it is just another tree transformation (ultrametric
  matrices are positive semi-definite; @dellacherie2014).
* On trees with **fossil tips**, or phylograms without a clock, only
  *completely monotone* functions are guaranteed, such as the exponential,
  which is the Ornstein–Uhlenbeck kernel [@schoenberg1938; @feragen2015].
  Squared-exponential and Matérn kernels can fail.

The smallest eigenvalue of the kernel matrix tells us directly. Below,
three trees: ultrametric, ultrametric with some tips shortened to make them
"fossils", and a random tree without a clock.

```{r validity, fig.height = 3.8}
set.seed(3)
ultra <- ape::rphylo(60, birth = 1, death = 0)
fossil <- ape::rphylo(60, birth = 1, death = 0.6, fossils = TRUE)  # keeps extinct lineages
noclock <- ape::rtree(60)
trees <- list("ultrametric" = ultra, "with fossil tips" = fossil,
              "no clock" = noclock)
sapply(trees, ape::Ntip)

phis <- c("exponential", "matern32", "matern52", "sqexp")
ells <- 10^seq(-2, 1, length.out = 40)
min_eig <- function(tree, phi, ell) {
  K <- kernel_matrix(k_dist(phi = phi), tree, list(dist1 = list(ell = ell)))
  min(eigen(K, symmetric = TRUE, only.values = TRUE)$values)
}

op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 3), mar = c(4, 4, 2.5, 0.5), mgp = c(2.4, 0.7, 0))
for (nm in names(trees)) {
  H <- max(ape::node.depth.edgelength(trees[[nm]]))
  ev <- sapply(phis, function(p) sapply(ells * H, function(l) min_eig(trees[[nm]], p, l)))
  matplot(ells, ev, type = "l", lty = 1, lwd = 2.2, col = cols, log = "x",
          ylim = c(min(-0.1, ev), 0.15), las = 1, bty = "l", main = nm, font.main = 1,
          xlab = "length-scale (tree heights)",
          ylab = if (nm == "ultrametric") "smallest eigenvalue" else "")
  abline(h = 0, lty = 2, col = "grey40")
  if (nm == "ultrametric")
    legend("bottomleft", c("exponential (OU)", "Matern 3/2", "Matern 5/2",
                           "squared exp."), col = cols, lwd = 2.2, bty = "n", cex = 0.85)
}
par(op)
```

`kernel_check()` applies these rules for you, and checks numerically where
validity is not guaranteed:

```{r validity-check}
kernel_check(k_bm() + k_dist(phi = "sqexp") + k_white(), fossil)
kernel_check(k_bm() + k_dist(phi = "exponential") + k_white(), fossil)
```

An invalid "kernel" should be replaced, not rescued by adding jitter to the
diagonal, which silently changes the model being fitted.

## When two kernels are the same model

Different processes can imply exactly the same distribution for the tips.
On an ultrametric tree, a single-optimum OU process with a fixed root has
the same kernel as an *accelerating* early-burst (ACDC) model with rate
$r = 2\alpha$. With extant species alone the two cannot be told apart, but
fossil tips separate them. The equivalence has been noted before
[@ho2014intrinsic; @uyeda2015comparative; @murrell2018].

```{r equivalence, fig.height = 3.8}
alpha <- 1.5
pair <- function(tree) {
  H <- max(ape::node.depth.edgelength(tree))
  list(ou = kernel_matrix(k_ou(root = "fixed"), tree,
                          list(ou1 = list(alpha = alpha))),
       eb = kernel_matrix(k_eb(upper = 10), tree,
                          list(eb1 = list(sigma = exp(-alpha * H), rate = 2 * alpha))))
}
m_ultra <- pair(ultra)
m_fossil <- pair(fossil)
max(abs(m_ultra$ou - m_ultra$eb))      # identical on the ultrametric tree

op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2.5, 1), mgp = c(2.4, 0.7, 0))
for (x in list(list(m_ultra, "ultrametric tree"), list(m_fossil, "with fossil tips"))) {
  plot(x[[1]]$eb, x[[1]]$ou, pch = 16, cex = 0.5, las = 1, bty = "l",
       col = adjustcolor(cols[1], 0.35), main = x[[2]], font.main = 1,
       xlab = "accelerating early burst (r = 2 alpha)", ylab = "OU, fixed root")
  abline(0, 1, col = cols[2], lwd = 1.5)
}
par(op)
```

`kernel_equivalent()` asks the same question for any pair of kernels. For
each parameter setting of the first kernel it searches over *all*
parameters of the second for the closest tip distribution, and reports the
Kullback–Leibler divergence: the expected log-likelihood ratio in favour of
the first kernel for one data set simulated from it. With the mean unknown
(the default), only contrasts between species are compared, as in REML.

```{r equivalent}
kernel_equivalent(k_ou(root = "fixed"), k_eb(upper = 50), ultra, n_grid = 4)
```

The early-burst rate it finds is exactly $2\alpha$. On the tree with fossil
tips the answer depends on how strong selection is:

```{r equivalent-curve, fig.height = 3.8}
alphas <- 10^seq(-1, 1.2, length.out = 10)
kl_curve <- function(tree) {
  H <- max(ape::node.depth.edgelength(tree))
  sapply(alphas, function(a) kernel_equivalent(
    k_ou(root = "fixed"), k_eb(upper = 100), tree,
    pars = list(ou1 = list(alpha = a / H)))$KL)
}
kl <- cbind(ultrametric = kl_curve(ultra), "with fossil tips" = kl_curve(fossil))
op <- par(mar = c(4, 4.5, 1, 1), mgp = c(2.6, 0.7, 0))
matplot(alphas, pmax(kl, 1e-8), log = "xy", type = "b", pch = 19, lty = 1, lwd = 2,
        col = cols[c(1, 2)], las = 1, bty = "l", yaxt = "n",
        xlab = "OU selection strength (alpha x tree height)",
        ylab = "KL to the best early burst")
axis(2, at = 10^c(-8, -4, 0), labels = c("1e-8", "1e-4", "1"), las = 1)
abline(h = 1, lty = 2, col = "grey50")
legend("topleft", colnames(kl), col = cols[c(1, 2)], lwd = 2, pch = 19, bty = "n")
par(op)
```

On the ultrametric tree the two models coincide for every strength of
selection (KL at numerical zero). With fossil tips they separate once
selection is strong; above the dashed line one data set of this size gives,
on average, more than one log-likelihood unit of evidence for the true
model. The search is numerical, so a large KL means only that no
equivalent parameter values were found; check that the best parameters of
the second kernel are not at their bounds (the `k2_at_bound` column).

## Why branch-wise kernels scale

Branch-wise kernels never need the $N \times N$ matrix: the likelihood is
evaluated by a single pass over the edges, and leave-one-out densities by
two. Even with the pruning loop in plain R, and the dense Cholesky in
optimised linear-algebra libraries, the difference is large beyond a few
hundred species:

```{r timing, fig.height = 4.2}
# average over repeated evaluations, so that fast calls are measurable
time_it <- function(f, n = 10) system.time(for (i in seq_len(n)) f())[["elapsed"]] / n
sizes <- c(100, 200, 400, 800, 1600, 3200)
timing <- t(sapply(sizes, function(n) {
  tree <- ape::rcoal(n)
  y <- rnorm(n)
  names(y) <- tree$tip.label
  dense <- if (n <= 1600) {
    K <- kernel_matrix(k_bm() + k_white(), tree)
    yy <- y[rownames(K)]
    time_it(function() { U <- chol(K); backsolve(U, yy, transpose = TRUE) })
  } else NA
  c(pruning = time_it(function() kernel_loglik(k_bm() + k_white(), tree, y)),
    dense = dense)
}))
op <- par(mar = c(4.5, 5, 1, 1), mgp = c(3.2, 0.7, 0))
matplot(sizes, timing * 1000, log = "xy", type = "b", pch = 19, yaxt = "n",
        lty = 1, lwd = 2, col = cols[c(1, 2)], bty = "l",
        xlab = "number of species", ylab = "time per likelihood (ms)")
axis(2, at = 10^(-1:3), labels = c("0.1", "1", "10", "100", "1000"), las = 1)
legend("topleft", c("pruning, O(N)", "dense Cholesky, O(N^3)"),
       col = cols[c(1, 2)], lwd = 2, pch = 19, bty = "n")
par(op)
```

In the compiled Stan programs that `phylo_gp()` generates, the same
algorithm keeps each gradient evaluation linear in the number of species,
which is what makes kernels with thousands of latent rates practical.
